nameOfficial: République du Tchad (Republic of Chad, جمهورية تشاد)
summary: Chad takes its name from its lake, and what that name meant is not established: Kanuri uses it as a proper name and has other words for "lake", and Nachtigal traced it not to Kanembu but to Buduma, the language of the islands. Kingdoms of Kanem and Bornu, Sara chieftaincies: its territory joins the Sahara, the Sahel and the savannah. The Sara, Chadian Arabs, Kanembu and Toubou bring Sudanic and Saharan traditions together there.
etymology:
The country takes its name from Lake Chad, around which Kanem and then Bornu were built. What the word designated before it designated this lake is not established, and the explanation commonly given, a Kanembu word meaning "large expanse of water", is not found in any of the sources consulted.

The first Europeans to reach the lake, Dixon Denham and Hugh Clapperton, use the form "Chad" in 1826 without ever translating it. Sigismund Koelle, the first lexicographer of Kanuri, writes in 1854 that Tsade is "the well-known freshwater lake, which other peoples also call Tsad": he treats it as a proper name and gives it no meaning. Norbert Cyffer's English-Kanuri dictionary, in 1994, keeps Sáde for Lake Chad but renders "lake" as kulúwu or njî kúra, literally the great water. In other words, Kanuri does not use that word to say a lake. Gustav Nachtigal, who stayed in the region in the 1870s, traced the term to Buduma, the language of the island inhabitants, with the sense of a great accumulation of water: this is neither the same language nor the same people as Kanembu.

The mechanism often invoked, that of the traveller who asks the name of a place and is told what the thing is, is documented by none of the authors read here for Lake Chad. Denham reports no exchange of this kind. To present it as the history of the name would be a reconstruction.
nameOriginActor: The name is that of the lake, taken up by the French colonial administration to designate the territory in the early twentieth century, then kept at independence. Who named the lake, and in which language, remains disputed: Kanuri uses the word as a proper name without translating it, Nachtigal traced it to Buduma, and no source consulted attributes it to Kanembu.

historicalNames.antiquity: Presence of Saharan and Central Sudanic peoples in the region. Contacts with Egyptian and Nubian civilisations. The region was known as "Kanem" to Arab geographers.
historicalNames.middleAges: Presence of Saharan peoples (Kanembu, Toubou) and Central Sudanic peoples (Sara) in the region. Development of the Kingdom of Kanem (eighth to fourteenth centuries) and of the Kingdom of Bornu (fourteenth to nineteenth centuries). The region was known as "Kanem" or "Bornu" to Arab geographers.
historicalNames.precolonial: Presence of Saharan peoples (Kanembu, Toubou), Central Sudanic peoples (Sara), and Arabs in the region. Development of the Kingdom of Kanem-Bornu. The region was known as "Kanem" or "Bornu" to Arab geographers, but the local populations had their own names for it.
historicalNames.colonization: 1900-1960: French Colony of Chad. Development of the plantation economy (cotton, groundnuts), mining, nationalist movements (twentieth century). The name "Chad" was made official by the French colonisers.
historicalNames.contemporary: 1960: Independence (11 August 1960), proclamation of the Republic of Chad. The name "Chad" is official.

majorPeoples.name: Sara
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: "Sara" is the autonym. No pejorative term is known. Majority Central Sudanic group, originating in Chad and the Central African Republic.

majorPeoples.name: Arabes tchadiens
exonyms: "Baggara" (historical term for certain nomadic Arab groups)
majorPeoples.mainRegion: Central and eastern Chad, desert zones
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: "Al-'Arab" (العرب) is the autonym. The term "Baggara" (cattle herders) is historical and descriptive. Semitic group, descendants of Arab immigrants who arrived from the seventh century onwards, with intermixing with local populations.

majorPeoples.name: Kanembu
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: "Kanembu" is the autonym. No pejorative term is known. Saharan group, historically linked to the Kingdom of Kanem-Bornu.

majorPeoples.name: Toubou
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: "Toubou" is the autonym. "Teda" and "Daza" are the names of the subgroups. No pejorative term is known. Saharan group, originating in Chad, Niger and Libya, in the central Sahara region.

majorPeoples.name: Autres groupes
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: Each group has its own autonym. No pejorative term is known.

culture.culturalTraditions: Central Sudanic traditions (Sara): traditional music, traditional dance, oral poetry, crafts (pottery, weaving), agriculture. Arab traditions (Chadian Arabs): traditional music, traditional dance, oral poetry, crafts, pastoral herding. Saharan traditions (Kanembu, Toubou): traditional music, traditional dance, oral poetry, crafts, pastoral herding, trans-Saharan trade. Varied traditional festivals. Ceremonies of passage, initiation rites, traditional celebrations. Chadian culture is rich and preserved, with a strong oral tradition (poetry).
culture.dominantReligions: Sunni Islam (majority, about 55%), Christianity (about 40%, mainly Catholicism), traditional African religions (frequent syncretism, about 5%)
culture.lifestyles: Agriculture (cotton, groundnuts, sorghum, millet, food crops), livestock herding (cattle, goats, sheep, camels, nomadic and semi-nomadic way of life), fishing (Lake Chad, an important source of protein), mining (oil, gold), trade and urban activities (urban areas, N'Djamena). Limited urbanisation. Economy based on agriculture (cotton, groundnuts), pastoral herding, and oil extraction (a major sector). Chad is one of the poorest countries in Africa, with a very low HDI and an economy dependent on oil.
culture.socialOrganization: Multiethnic and multicultural society. Traditional family structures (patrilineal). Community organisation (tribal groupings, clans, chieftaincies). Modern state structures (republic, but political instability and recent conflicts). Democratic political system, but political instability and recent conflicts (civil war, rebellions, coups d'état).
culture.regionalRelations: Relations with Central Africa (ECCAS, African Union), relations with the Sahel (G5 Sahel), relations with the Middle East (Arab League), relations with Europe (European Union, France), relations with the United States. Chad is a member of ECCAS, the African Union and the Arab League.

historicalFacts.middleAges: Presence of Saharan peoples (Kanembu, Toubou) and Central Sudanic peoples (Sara) in the region. Development of the Kingdom of Kanem (eighth to fourteenth centuries) and of the Kingdom of Bornu (fourteenth to nineteenth centuries). The region was known as "Kanem" or "Bornu" to Arab geographers.

historicalFacts.colonization: 1900-1960: French Colony of Chad, development of the plantation economy (cotton, groundnuts), mining, nationalist movements (twentieth century).
historicalFacts.independenceStruggle: 1950s-1960: Nationalist movements, PPT (Chadian Progressive Party), independence (11 August 1960), proclamation of the Republic of Chad. François Tombalbaye becomes the first president.
historicalFacts.postIndependence: Republic of Chad (1960), presidency of François Tombalbaye (1960-1975, authoritarian regime, single party), coup d'état (1975), civil war (1965-1979, 2005-2010), presidency of Hissène Habré (1982-1990, authoritarian regime, crimes against humanity), presidency of Idriss Déby (1990-2021, authoritarian regime, rebellions), death of Idriss Déby (2021), military transition, presidency of Mahamat Idriss Déby (since 2021). Fragile political stability, state in transition, recent conflicts (civil war, rebellions, coups d'état), economic development (agriculture, herding, oil extraction). Chad is one of the poorest countries in Africa, with a very low HDI and an economy dependent on oil.

sources.title: Sigismund Wilhelm Koelle, African Native Literature, or Proverbs, Tales, Fables and Historical Fragments in the Kanuri or Bornu Language, Londres, Church Missionary House, 1854
sources.notes: Describes Tsade as the well-known freshwater lake, which other peoples also call Tsad. The word is treated as a proper name and receives no translation; the vocabulary has no entry glossing it. Note and vocabulary read in facsimile on 9 September 2026.

sources.title: Norbert Cyffer, English–Kanuri Dictionary, Cologne, 1994
sources.notes: Gives Sáde for Lake Chad, and kulúwu or njî kúra for the common noun "lake". The work is verified in the catalogue; these two entries are taken from a discussion by linguists that cites them, as the dictionary itself was not consulted.

sources.title: Gustav Nachtigal, Saharâ und Sûdân. Ergebnisse sechsjähriger Reisen in Afrika, Berlin, Weidmann, à partir de 1879
sources.notes: Traces the name of the lake to Buduma, the language of the island inhabitants, with the sense of a great accumulation of water. The work is verified in the catalogue; the passage was not read and is reported by a discussion among linguists.

sources.title: « Lake Chad », Language Hat, 5 décembre 2017, et ses commentaires
sources.notes: Discussion among linguists. It is the origin of the entries cited here from Cyffer's dictionary and of the attribution to Buduma in Nachtigal, and it also notes the form cádù recorded by Roger Blench in Manga Kanuri. It concludes that nobody knows with certainty what the word designated. Page read on 9 September 2026.
